data.title: Putin's United Russia wins tightly controlled wartime election
data.incipit: The Kremlin-backed United Russia party has secured victory in Russia's parliamentary election, taking more than half of the vote, according to preliminary results reported by Russian news agencies.United...
data.body: The Kremlin-backed United Russia party has secured victory in Russia's parliamentary election, taking more than half of the vote, according to preliminary results reported by Russian news agencies. United Russia secured 57.9% of the vote after more than 50% of ballots have been counted, Interfax reported, citing the election commission. Predictions had placed the party, which has ruled for more than 20 years, below 50%. According to preliminary estimates, the party was set to win 309 of the 450 seats in the State Duma, including direct mandates, nine more seats than are needed to amend the constitution, Novaya Gazeta reported. The election was Russia's first parliamentary vote since President Vladimir Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and was widely seen as a test of public backing for the war. The vote has been dismissed by democracy watchdogs, Western governments and Kremlin opponents as neither free nor fair, with critics accusing the authorities of excluding genuine opposition and tightly controlling the political landscape. The anti-war Yabloko party was barred from the election, while all parties represented in the outgoing parliament are considered loyal to the Kremlin and support Russia's war against Ukraine. The Communist Party won 13.8% of the vote, followed by the ultranationalist LDPR on 8.8% and New People on 7.9%, according to the initial results. A Just Russia was on 5.1%, putting all four parties on course to return to the State Duma. Official figures put turnout at more than 56%, higher than in the 2021 parliamentary election. Figures provided by Russia's electoral authorities cannot be independently verified. Despite Ukraine's protests, the election was held for the first time in the Russian-controlled parts of the annexed Ukrainian regions of Luhansk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhya and Kherson. The Black Sea peninsula of Crimea, which was annexed back in 2014, was once again included. Allegations of electoral violations Yabloko, which was initially approved to stand before being removed from the ballot, and the traditionally strong Communist Party both complained that hundreds of their observers had been prevented from monitoring polling stations. Civil servants also reported being pressured to vote, while there were allegations of ballot stuffing, as in previous Russian elections. Some voters complained that they had not received polling cards and had been registered for online voting without their knowledge. Electronic voting in Russia has faced criticism over a lack of transparency and concerns about possible manipulation. More than 110 million Russians were eligible to elect the 450 members of the new State Duma in the three-day vote. In addition to the Duma election, deputies were also elected to regional parliaments in eight regions. According to the election commission, a total of around 2,200 elections took place at various levels of government.
